title: Writing Functions
description: Give a block of code a name so you can run it whenever you like.

content.value: `int main()` is a **function**: a named block of instructions. Write it once, then run it by writing its name and `()`. That is called **calling** the function.

content.text: A recipe keeps its steps in one place, under one name. You follow it whenever you need it. A function does the same for lines of code.

content.caption: The three banner lines are written once and printed twice. Change the banner and both copies change, because there is only one copy.

items.sub: `printBanner()` says what is about to happen. Three `cout` lines full of `=` do not.
Repeated code has to be fixed in every copy, and one copy always gets missed.
When `main` is a list of calls, you can read the shape of the whole program on one screen.

content.question: What is the main reason to write a function?
options: To make the program run faster
Write steps once, then reuse them by name
To repeat a line for ever
content.explain: A function keeps a group of steps in one place under one name. You call the name instead of copying lines, and a fix only needs one edit.

parts.label: name
parts.note: lowerCamelCase, like a variable. It should read as an instruction.

parts.label: parameters
parts.note: Empty brackets: the function needs nothing from the caller.

content.title: Anatomy of a function header
content.caption: Then the body sits between `{ }`, just like `main`'s.

items.sub: Its return type is `int`, which is why it ends with `return 0;`: it hands 0 back to the system, meaning "all went well".
`printBanner`, `drawLine`, `askAge`. If you cannot name it in two or three words, it does too many jobs.
In this course, functions sit above `main`. The next tab shows why.

content.value: If a function needs a comment to explain what it does, try a better name first. A well named function is the comment.
content.title: Names first

content.question: Which line correctly starts a function named `wave` that hands nothing back?
content.explain: Return type `void`, then the name, then the brackets, then the opening brace: `void wave() {`.

content.value: The compiler reads your file once, top to bottom. When it reaches a call, it must already have seen that function's name.

items.title: Does not compile
items.text: g++ says `'sayHello' was not declared in this scope` and points at the call.

items.title: Compiles
items.text: Fix 1: move the whole function above `main`.

content.title: Below main vs above main
content.caption: Nothing is wrong with the function itself. It is simply too far down the file.

Fix 2: a **prototype** is the first line of a function with `;` instead of a body. It promises the function exists. The full version with the body is the **definition**, and it can go anywhere below, in any order. The prototype must match the definition exactly.

content.value: Wrote a prototype but forgot the definition? The error is `undefined reference to 'sayHello()'`. It comes from the **linker**, the tool that joins the compiled pieces into one program, and means "you promised this function but never wrote it".
content.title: A different error

content.question: What is the line `void drawLine();` near the top of a file?
content.explain: A function's first line with a semicolon instead of a body is a prototype: a promise that the definition comes later.

content.value: A call is a detour. C++ leaves the line it is on, runs the whole function, then comes back to exactly where it left off.

steps.note: `main` runs first, as always, even though `step` is written above it.
A call. C++ leaves `main` and jumps into `step`.
The function ran out of lines, so C++ returns to `main`, just after the call.

content.title: Watch C++ jump in and back
content.outro: Nothing is skipped and nothing runs twice. A function written first in the file only runs when it is called.

content.caption: A function can call another one. `drawLine` sits above `printReport` for the same reason both sit above `main`: a caller must come after the function, or have a prototype.

content.question: What does this print?
content.explain: C++ jumps into `hi` at the call, prints `B`, then comes back and carries on with `C`.

content.caption: The banner never appears. A bare name only mentions the function, it does not call it, and g++ at most gives a warning that is easy to miss. If a function seems never to run, check the brackets first.

items.title: Function inside main
items.text: `a function-definition is not allowed here before '{' token`. Functions are neighbours of `main`, never part of it.

items.title: Fixed
items.text: The function moved above `main`, and the call has its `()`.

content.title: Calls need brackets, functions live outside main

content.value: One misplaced function can produce several errors. Fix the **first** error and compile again: the rest are usually echoes of it.
content.title: Fix the first error first

content.question: A function `beep` is never printing anything. Which line is the likely bug?
content.explain: Without `()` the name is only mentioned, not called. It compiles, so the bug is silent.

practice.question: Write a function called printGoodbye that prints two lines, then call it twice from main.
Write drawLine so that it prints 20 dashes using a loop, then call it above and below the title in main.
This does not compile because main calls countToThree before the compiler has seen it. Fix it twice: once by moving the function, then (undo that) by adding a prototype.
Write a function runAll that calls drawLine, then sayHello, then drawLine. main should call only runAll.

quiz.question: What is a function?
options: A variable that holds several values
A named block of instructions you can run by calling its name
quiz.explain: `main` is one too. Naming a block lets you run it from anywhere, as often as you like.

quiz.question: `main` calls `sayHello()`, which is defined below `main` with no prototype. What happens?
options: A compile error: 'sayHello' was not declared in this scope
It works, because C++ reads the whole file first
It compiles but sayHello never runs
quiz.explain: The compiler reads top to bottom. Move the function above main, or put a prototype like `void sayHello();` above it.

quiz.question: What does `void` mean in `void printBanner()`?
options: The function takes no values in
The function hands nothing back to whoever called it
quiz.explain: `void` is the return type. The empty brackets are what say it takes nothing in.

quiz.question: What happens after a called function finishes?
options: The program carries on at the line right after the call
quiz.explain: A call is a detour, not a jump. C++ always comes back to where it left off.

quiz.question: What does the line `printBanner;` do?
options: Nothing: without brackets it only mentions the function, it does not call it
It calls the function, the brackets are optional
It always stops the program from compiling
quiz.explain: It compiles, at most with a warning, and quietly does nothing. The round brackets are what make a call.
